text: William Steinitz (born Wilhelm Steinitz; May 14, 1836 – August 12, 1900) was a Bohemian-Austrian, and later American, chess player who served as the first World Chess Champion from 1886 to 1894. He was also a prominent chess writer and theoretician. Commentators have debated whether Steinitz could be considered the world champion as early as 1866, and he lost his title to Emanuel Lasker in 1894, with a rematch loss in 1896–97. Despite low statistical ratings due to long breaks from competitive play, an analysis using rating systems shows he was one of the most dominant players in chess history, remaining unbeaten in match play for 32 years, from 1862 to 1894. Steinitz initially played in the attacking "Romantic" style common in the 1860s, but in 1873 introduced a new positional style, which was initially controversial and labeled "cowardly" by some, though it proved capable of setting up fierce attacks. He defended his ideas vigorously, leading to a bitter and abusive debate known as the "Ink War," which by the early 1890s had resulted in widespread acceptance of his positional approach, with his successor, Emanuel Lasker, acknowledging his influence. Traditional portrayals of Steinitz depict him as ill-tempered and aggressive, but recent research indicates he maintained long and friendly relationships with players and chess organizations, notably co-operating with the American Chess Congress from 1888 to 1889 to establish rules for future world championships. He was unskilled at managing money and lived in poverty throughout his life. Born in the Jewish ghetto of Prague (then in Bohemia, part of the Austrian Empire), the youngest of thirteen sons of tailor Josef-Salomon Steinitz, he began playing chess at age 12. After studying Talmud in his youth and studying mathematics at the Vienna Polytechnic from 1857 to 1859, he rapidly improved, winning first place in the 1861 Vienna City championship with a score of 30/31 and earning the nickname "the Austrian Morphy," becoming the strongest player in Austria. He represented Austria in the 1862 London tournament, placing sixth but winning the brilliancy prize for a win over Augustus Mongredien, and then challenged and defeated Serafino Dubois in a match (five wins, one draw, three losses), which encouraged him to turn professional and settle in London. In 1862–63, he defeated Joseph Henry Blackburne (a future top-ten player) decisively, and later beat Frederick Deacon, Mongredien, and Valentine Green. In 1866, he defeated Adolf Anderssen, the world's strongest active player at the time, in a match with eight wins and six losses (no draws), which was a hard-fought contest that ended with Steinitz winning the last two games after a 6–6 tie after 12 games. The prize was £100 for the winner (equivalent to about £57,500 in 2007), and £20 for Anderssen. Following this, he beat Henry Bird in 1866 (seven wins, five losses, five draws) and Johannes Zukertort in 1872 (seven wins, four draws, one loss), who had previously beaten Anderssen in 1871. In tournament play, he took third place at Paris 1867 and second at Dundee (1867) and Baden-Baden (1870), behind Anderssen but ahead of Blackburne, Paulsen, and others. His first tournament victory ahead of Anderssen was in Vienna 1873, where he tied with Blackburne and won the play-off, marking the start of a 25-game winning streak. Between 1873 and 1882, he played no tournaments and only one match (a 7–0 win against Blackburne in 1876), with his other games being in simultaneous and blindfold exhibitions, which were a key source of income. During this time, he worked as a chess journalist for The Field, Britain's leading sports magazine, and his commentaries sparked heated debates, especially with Zukertort and Leopold Hoffer in The Chess Monthly, escalating into the "Ink War" in 1881. In 1882, James Mason challenged Steinitz, accusing him of cowardice for refusing to play Zukertort, and Steinitz insisted on a high stake of at least £150 per player (equivalent to £19,083 in 2023), which Mason refused. Mason later agreed to play Zukertort for £100 per player but postponed the match. Some commentators suggested that Zukertort, who had notable tournament wins, should be considered world champion after Steinitz's loss in a tournament, with The Chess Player's Chronicle in July 1883 stating that Zukertort "becomes champion" temporarily. Zukertort reportedly told Steinitz, "You are not a chessplayer, but a Jew." In 1882, Steinitz returned to serious competition in the Vienna tournament, tying for first with Szymon Winawer and drawing the play-off. From December 1882 to May 1883, he visited the United States, receiving enthusiastic reception, playing exhibitions, casual games, and winning three serious matches—against Alexander Sellman (both wins) and Cuban champion Celso Golmayo Zúpide (match abandoned when Steinitz led 8–1–1). His hosts arranged a visit to New Orleans, where Paul Morphy lived. In 1883, he finished second in the London tournament behind Zukertort, who finished three points ahead, and again some commentators suggested Zukertort should be champion, while others insisted a match between Steinitz and Zukertort was needed. In 1883, shortly after the London tournament, Steinitz moved to New York City, where he lived for the rest of his life, though not yet a U.S. citizen. He became a U.S. citizen on November 23, 1888, after five years in New York, and changed his first name from Wilhelm to William. In 1887, the American Chess Congress began drafting regulations for future world championship contests, and Steinitz supported this effort, writing in his magazine that he was no longer fit to be champion and would not hold the title forever. In 1888, the Havana Chess Club offered to sponsor a match between Steinitz and a selected opponent; he nominated Mikhail Chigorin on the condition the invitation not be presented as a challenge, and the match was limited to 20 games. Steinitz opposed fixed-length matches for world championships, as they allowed a player to take a lead and play for draws, and he supported the American Chess Congress's project. The match in Havana (January–February 1889) was won by Steinitz (ten wins, one draw, six losses). The American Chess Congress proposed that the winner of a New York 1889 tournament would be world champion temporarily and must face a challenge from second or third place within a month. Steinitz refused to play in the tournament and would not challenge unless the second and third-place players failed to do so. The tournament resulted in a tie between Chigorin and Max Weiss, with a four-draw play-off, and Weiss conceding the title to Chigorin, while Isidor Gunsberg, the third-place finisher, was prepared to play for the title. A Steinitz–Gunsberg match in 1890 ended with a 10½–8½ victory for Steinitz. The experiment was not repeated, and Steinitz's last three matches were private arrangements. In 1891, the Saint Petersburg Chess Society and Havana Chess Club offered another Steinitz–Chigorin match for the world championship, which was played in Havana in 1892 and won by Steinitz (ten wins, five draws, eight losses). Dr. Siegbert Tarrasch declined a 1892 challenge due to medical commitments. Around this time, Steinitz publicly announced his retirement but changed his mind when Emanuel Lasker, 32 years younger and relatively untested, challenged him. Lasker had previously been refused a non-title challenge by Tarrasch, who was the world's dominant tournament player at the time. Initially, Lasker wanted $5,000 per side, and the match was agreed at $3,000 per side, but Steinitz reduced the stakes due to financial difficulties, settling on $2,000 each (equivalent to about $114,000 in 2016 values), which was publicly praised as sportsmanship but may have been necessary for Steinitz. The match took place in 1894 in New York, Philadelphia, and Montreal, Canada, with a 32-year age difference between the players—the largest in world championship history and still the largest today. Steinitz had previously declared he would win without doubt, but Lasker won the first game. Steinitz won the second and maintained balance until the sixth, but Lasker won games seven through eleven, and Steinitz requested a one-week rest. When the match resumed, Steinitz looked in better form.

Initz agreed to a series of reductions in stakes when Lasker found it difficult to raise funds, resulting in a final payment of $2,000 each, which was less than in some of Steinitz's earlier matches; the combined final stake of $4,000 would be worth about $114,000 at 2016 values. Although this was publicly praised as an act of sportsmanship, Steinitz may have desperately needed the money. The match took place in 1894 at venues in New York, Philadelphia, and Montreal, Canada, and featured the largest age difference between combatants in world championship history—32 years—which remains unbroken today. Steinitz had previously declared he would win without doubt, but it came as a shock when Lasker won the first game; Steinitz responded by winning the second and maintained balance until the sixth. Lasker then won all games from the seventh to the eleventh, and Steinitz requested a one-week rest. Upon resuming, Steinitz won the 13th and 14th games, but Lasker regained the lead in the 15th and 16th, and Steinitz could not recover, resulting in Lasker winning with ten wins, five losses, and four draws. Some commentators believed Steinitz's habit of playing "experimental" moves in serious competition contributed significantly to his downfall. After losing the title, Steinitz played more frequently in tournaments; he won at New York City 1894 and placed fifth at Hastings 1895, winning the first brilliancy prize for his game against Curt von Bardeleben. At Saint Petersburg 1895, a strong four-player, multi-round-robin event with Lasker, Chigorin, and Pillsbury, he finished second behind Lasker. His results declined afterward: sixth in Nuremberg 1896, fifth in Cologne 1898, and tenth in London 1899. In early 1896, Steinitz defeated Emanuel Schiffers in a match, winning 6 games, drawing 1, and losing 4. From November 1896 to January 1897, he played a return match with Lasker in Moscow, winning only 2 games, drawing 5, and losing 10—this was the last world chess championship match for eleven years. Shortly after, Steinitz suffered a mental breakdown and was confined for 40 days in a Moscow sanatorium, where he played chess with inmates. There is ongoing debate among chess writers about whether Steinitz's reign as World Chess Champion began in 1866, when he beat Anderssen, or in 1886, when he defeated Zukertort. In April 1894, the British Chess Magazine described Steinitz as holding the chess championship of the world for 28 years, though there is no evidence he claimed the title in 1866, and he had claimed to be champion since his 1880s victory over Anderssen. It is suggested he could not claim the title while Paul Morphy was alive, as Morphy had defeated Anderssen 8–3 in 1858 and retired in 1859, dying in 1884. The 1886 match between Steinitz and Zukertort was the first explicitly described as being for the World Championship, though Howard Staunton and Paul Morphy had been unofficially called "World Chess Champion" in the mid-19th century. One organizer of the 1851 London International tournament referred to the event as being for "the baton of the World's Chess Champion," and Ludwig Bledow suggested in 1845 organizing a world championship in Germany. Some commentators described Steinitz as "the champion" after his 1872 victory over Zukertort, but in the late 1870s and early 1880s, both Steinitz and Zukertort were regarded as champions, and the 1886 match was seen as resolving conflicting claims rather than creating the title. George Alcock MacDonnell hailed Joseph Blackburne as "World Champion" in 1881, George Henry Mackenzie as having "won the Chess Championship of the World" in 1887, and Isidore Gunsberg as "among the champions of the world" after his 1888 win at "Bradford Place." Steinitz regarded MacDonnell as "one of my bitterest and most untruthful persecutors." Steinitz lived with Caroline Golder (born 1846) in the 1860s, and their only daughter, Flora, was born in 1866; Flora died in 1888 at age 21, and Caroline died in 1892. He married his second wife a few years later and had two children with her. In 1897, he dedicated a pamphlet to the memory of his first wife and daughter. In February 1897, The New York Times prematurely reported his death in a New York mental asylum. Some authors claim he contracted syphilis, which may have contributed to his mental breakdowns. In the months before his death, he spent time in institutions due to failing mental health. Before confinement, Steinitz was attempting to publish an essay on the emancipation of Austrian Jews and attributed his symptoms entirely to mental fatigue. His chess activities did not yield significant financial rewards, and he died a pauper in the Manhattan State Hospital (Wards Island) on August 12, 1900, from a heart attack. Steinitz is buried in the Cemetery of the Evergreens in Brooklyn, New York. His second wife and their two young children were still alive at the time of his death. The book of the Hastings 1895 tournament described Steinitz as a strong theoretician and writer with a powerful pen, who strives to be fair to friends and foes but sometimes fails to see that he is like many others. He is described as having a fine intellect and being extremely fond of chess, often losing sight of other considerations. His play up to and including 1872 mirrored that of his contemporaries: sharp, aggressive, and full of sacrificial play, which led to his rise as "world number one" after beating Adolf Anderssen in 1866 and confirming his position by defeating Zukertort in 1872 and winning the 1872 London International tournament (Zukertort had claimed second place by beating Anderssen in 1871). In 1873, Steinitz's style changed, prioritizing positional elements such as pawn structure, space, knight outposts, and the advantage of two bishops. Although he often accepted difficult defensive positions to demonstrate his theories, he also showed that his methods could support powerful attacks. Lasker summarized the new style as: "In the beginning of the game ignore the search for combinations, abstain from violent moves, aim for small advantages, accumulate them, and only after having attained these ends search for the combination—and then with all the power of will and intellect, because then the combination must exist, however deeply hidden." Steinitz stated he had been thinking along these lines for years, citing Paulsen's games at the 1862 London Congress as a key influence. During his nine-year layoff from tournaments (1873–1882) and later in his career, he used chess writings to present his theories—writing for The Field in the UK from 1873 to 1882, founding the International Chess Magazine in New York in 1885 and editing it until 1891, and editing the book of the 1889 New York tournament (won by Chigorin and Weiss), which was designed to produce his successor as World Champion. Many writers found his new approach incomprehensible, boring, or even cowardly; Adolf Anderssen criticized him as a "pick-pocket" who wins by stealing a pawn. However, in his 1886 match against Zukertort, Steinitz clearly played at a higher level, outmaneuvering Zukertort through positional principles despite Zukertort's superior attacking ability. By the 1890–91 match against Gunsberg, some commentators began to understand and appreciate his theories. Before the 1894 match with Lasker, even The New York Times, which had previously attacked his play and character, paid tribute to his record, theories, and sportsmanship in agreeing to the most difficult match of his career despite his intention to retire. By the end of his career, Steinitz was more highly esteemed as a theoretician than as a player; the Hastings 1895 tournament comments focus on his theories and writings, and Lasker explicitly stated, "He was a thinker worthy of a seat in the halls of a University. A player, as the world believed he was, he was not; his studious temperament made that impossible; and thus he was conquered by a player." As a result of his play and writings, Steinitz, along with Paul Morphy, is considered by many commentators the founder of modern chess. Lasker, who succeeded him, wrote, "I who vanquished him must see to it that his great achievement, his theories should find justice, and I must avenge the wrongs he suffered." Vladimir Kramnik emphasized Steinitz's role as a pioneer in chess theory, stating he was the first to realize that chess, despite being complex, obeys common principles, though he was an experimenter rather than a founder of a complete theory. Steinitz was the main chess correspondent of The Field from 1873 to 1882, using it to present his strategic ideas. In 1885, he founded the International Chess Magazine in New York and edited it until 1891. He wrote articles on Paul Morphy, who died in 1884, and authored the book of the 1889 New York tournament, annotating all 432 games, and published the textbook The Modern Chess Instructor in 1889. He also allegedly wrote a pamphlet entitled Capital, Labor, and Charity while confined at River Crest Sanitarium in New York during his final months. Statistical rating systems are unkind to Steinitz; "Warriors of the Mind" ranks him 47th, below several obscure Soviet grandmasters, and Chessmetrics places him only 15th on its all-time list. Chessmetrics penalizes players who play infrequently; opportunities for competitive chess were rare in Steinitz's best years, and he had several long absences from play (1873–1876, 1876–1882, 1883–1886, 1886–1889). However, in 2005, Chessmetrics author Jeff Sonas found that Steinitz was ahead of his contemporaries in the 1870s compared to Bobby Fischer's peak (1970–1972), had the third-highest total number of years as world's top player (behind Lasker and Kasparov), and placed 7th in a comparison of how long players were ranked in the world's top three. Between his victory over Anderssen in 1866 and his loss to Lasker in 1894, Steinitz won all his "normal" matches, often by wide margins, and his worst tournament result in that 28-year period was third place in Paris (1867). He also lost two handicap matches and a match by telegraph in 1890 against Mikhail Chigorin, where Chigorin chose the openings and won both. The Edo rating system (1821–1937) places Steinitz third in peak rating, behind Jose Capablanca and Paul Morphy but ahead of Emanuel Lasker and Alexander Alekhine. Initially, Steinitz played in the all-out attacking style of contemporaries like Anderssen, then shifted to the positional style that dominated competitive chess in the 1870s and 1880s. Max Euwe noted that Steinitz aimed at positions with clear-cut features to which his theory was best applicable. He retained his capacity for brilliant attacks until the end; for example, at Hastings 1895 (when he was 59), he defeated von Bardeleben in a spectacular game where he deliberately exposed all his pieces to attack simultaneously (except his king). His significant weaknesses included playing "experimental" moves and entering unnecessarily difficult defensive positions in top-level games. Traditional accounts describe him as having a sharp tongue and violent temper, possibly due to his short stature (barely five feet) and congenital lameness. He admitted, "Like the Duke of Parma, I always hold the sword in one hand and the olive branch in the other," and could become abusive in published articles under provocation. He acknowledged early in his career that his frankness would offend and make enemies, and his brutally honest review of Wormald's The Chess Openings in 1875 confirmed this. His personal correspondence, articles, and third-party writings show he had long and friendly relationships with many in the chess world, including Ignác Kolisch, Mikhail Chigorin, Harry Nelson Pillsbury, Bernhard Horwitz, Amos Burn, and the Cuban and Russian chess communities. He also cooperated with the American Chess Congress in its project to regulate future world title contests that he had earned. Steinitz strove to be objective in his writings; for example, he attributed a poor tournament score by Henry Edward Bird to bad luck, despite not being a friend of Bird's, and was generous in praising great play by even his enemies. He also poked fun at his own rhetoric, such as saying he would rather die in America than live in England, and that he would rather lose a match in America than win one in England, but later concluded that he neither.

Steinitz was proven correct on two points. His personal letters, his own articles, and some third-party articles reveal that he maintained long and friendly relationships with numerous individuals and groups in the chess world, including Ignác Kolisch (one of his earliest sponsors), Mikhail Chigorin, Harry Nelson Pillsbury, Bernhard Horwitz, Amos Burn, and the Cuban and Russian chess communities. He also collaborated with the American Chess Congress on its initiative to regulate future world title contests, which he had won. Steinitz aimed for objectivity in his commentary on chess events; for instance, he credited Henry Edward Bird’s poor tournament performance to bad luck, despite considering Bird no friend, and he praised exceptional play even from his bitter rivals. He also self-ironized his own statements, such as saying he would rather die in America than live in England or lose a match in America than win one in England, later clarifying that he no longer meant to die or lose the match. During a joint simultaneous display in Russia around the time of the 1895–96 Saint Petersburg tournament, Emanuel Lasker and Steinitz formed an impromptu comedy double act. Although Steinitz valued honor in repaying debts, he struggled with financial management: he allowed a competitor to take many of his clients between 1862 and 1863, offered to play the 1886 world title match against Johannes Zukertort for free, and died in poverty in 1900, leaving his widow to survive by running a small shop.
